claim: Neurocysticercosis (NCC) is caused by infection of the brain by larvae of the parasitic cestode Taenia solium.
source: Neurocysticercosis (NCC) is caused by infection of the brain by larvae of the parasitic cestode Taenia solium.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge about NCC.

claim: NCC is the most prevalent parasitic infection of the central nervous system.
source: It is the most prevalent parasitic infection of the central nervous system and one of the leading causes of adult-acquired epilepsy worldwide.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction (Diop et al., 2003; Preux and Druet-Cabanac, 2005).

claim: NCC is one of the leading causes of adult-acquired epilepsy worldwide.
source: It is the most prevalent parasitic infection of the central nervous system and one of the leading causes of adult-acquired epilepsy worldwide.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations (Nash et al., 2013) in the introduction.

claim: Both whole cyst homogenate and excretory/secretory products of cestode larvae have an acute excitatory effect on neurons.
source: We found that both whole cyst homogenate and excretory/secretory products of cestode larvae have an acute excitatory effect on neurons, which can trigger seizure-like events in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings and calcium imaging shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Cestode larval products can trigger seizure-like events in vitro.
source: We found that both whole cyst homogenate and excretory/secretory products of cestode larvae have an acute excitatory effect on neurons, which can trigger seizure-like events in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 1F showing seizure-like activity.

claim: The excitatory effect of cestode larval products is mediated by glutamate receptor activation.
source: This effect was mediated by glutamate receptor activation but not by nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, acid-sensing ion channels, or Substance P.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3G-J where glutamate receptor blockers significantly reduced the depolarization response.

claim: The excitatory effect of cestode larval products is not mediated by nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
source: This effect was mediated by glutamate receptor activation but not by nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, acid-sensing ion channels, or Substance P.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3C-D showing that nAchR blockade did not affect the depolarization response.

claim: The excitatory effect of cestode larval products is not mediated by acid-sensing ion channels.
source: This effect was mediated by glutamate receptor activation but not by nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, acid-sensing ion channels, or Substance P.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3E-F showing that ASIC blockade did not affect the depolarization response.

claim: The excitatory effect of cestode larval products is not mediated by Substance P.
source: This effect was mediated by glutamate receptor activation but not by nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, acid-sensing ion channels, or Substance P.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A-B showing that Substance P application had no effect on membrane potential.

claim: The larval homogenate of Taenia crassiceps and Taenia solium contains high concentrations of glutamate and aspartate.
source: Glutamate-sensing fluorescent reporters (iGluSnFR) and amino acid assays revealed that the larval homogenate of the cestodes Taenia crassiceps and Taenia solium contained high concentrations of the amino acids glutamate and aspartate.
evidence: This is supported by iGluSnFR imaging data in Figure 4 and amino acid assay data in Figures 5D-E and 6C.

claim: Larvae of both Taenia crassiceps and Taenia solium produce and release excitatory amino acids into their immediate environment.
source: Furthermore, we found that larvae of both species consistently produce and release these excitatory amino acids into their immediate environment.
evidence: This is supported by de novo production data shown in Figures 5F and 6D.

claim: Perturbations in glutamatergic signalling may play a role in seizure generation in NCC.
source: Our findings suggest that perturbations in glutamatergic signalling may play a role in seizure generation in NCC.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings and inference from the data presented.

claim: The most common symptom of NCC is recurrent seizures.
source: The most common symptom of NCC is recurrent seizures (Garcia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Garcia et al., 2017.

claim: In T. solium endemic areas, 29% of people with epilepsy also had NCC.
source: In T. solium endemic areas, 29% of people with epilepsy also had NCC (Ndimubanzi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ndimubanzi et al., 2010.

claim: There have been no studies to date that investigated the direct, acute effects of cestode larval products on neurons.
source: As far as we are aware, there have been no studies to date that investigated the direct, acute effects of cestode larval products on neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: In NCC seizures may occur at any stage following initial infection.
source: In NCC seizures may occur at any stage following initial infection (Garcia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Garcia et al., 2017.

claim: Inflammatory processes in the brain play an important role in the development of recurrent seizures in NCC.
source: It is thought that inflammatory processes in the brain play an important role in the development of recurrent seizures (Vezzani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vezzani et al., 2016.

claim: Production of Substance P by peritoneal larval granulomas precipitated acute seizures in a study by Robinson et al.
source: One study by Robinson et al. found that production of the inflammatory molecule and neurotransmitter, Substance P, produced by peritoneal larval granulomas, precipitated acute seizures (Robinson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Robinson et al., 2012.

claim: Cestode larvae-derived factors are known to modulate the activation status of immunocytes such as microglia and dendritic cells.
source: Cestode larvae-derived factors are known to modulate the activation status of immunocytes such as microglia and dendritic cells (Sun et al., 2014; Vendelova et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sun et al., 2014 and Vendelova et al., 2016.

claim: Application of T. crassiceps homogenate elicited immediate, transient depolarization of the membrane voltage in recordings from rat, mouse, and human neurons.
source: Application of the homogenate (20-ms puff) elicited immediate, transient depolarization of the membrane voltage in recordings from rat, mouse, and human neurons (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Increasing the amount of T. crassiceps homogenate delivered resulted in increasingly large membrane depolarization, which could trigger single or multiple action potentials.
source: Increasing the amount of homogenate delivered by increasing the pressure applied to the ejection system resulted in increasingly large membrane depolarization, which could trigger single or multiple action potentials (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: A single, spatially restricted puff of T. crassiceps homogenate can elicit the onset of a regenerative seizure-like event lasting far longer than the puff itself.
source: Indeed, a current-clamp recording from a neuron in the same slice (Figure 1F, inset) indicates that a single, spatially restricted puff of T. crassiceps homogenate can elicit the onset of a regenerative SLE lasting far longer than the puff itself.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F inset.

claim: The K+ concentration of the T. crassiceps homogenate was 11.4 mM.
source: The K+ concentration of the T. crassiceps homogenate was 11.4 mM (N = 1, homogenate prepared from >100 larvae) as compared to 3.0 mM in our standard aCSF (N = 1).
evidence: This is based on direct measurement using a Roche Cobas 6000.

claim: Direct application of 11.4 mM K+ via puff pipette resulted in a modest median positive shift of only 0.72 mV in the membrane potential.
source: Direct application of 11.4 mM K+ via puff pipette during whole-cell current-clamp from rat CA3 pyramidal neurons resulted in a modest median positive shift of only 0.72 mV (IQR 0.51–1.04 mV, N = 8 from 4 slices, Figure 2B, C, Figure 2—source data 1) in the membrane potential
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: The depolarization caused by puffs of T. crassiceps homogenate (median 10.12 mV) was larger than that caused by 11.4 mM K+ (median 0.72 mV), although this did not reach statistical significance.
source: which was lower than the depolarization caused by puffs of T. crassiceps homogenate (median 10.12 mV, IQR 9.93–12.49 mV, N = 5 from 4 slices), although this did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.26, Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparison test, Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: T. crassiceps homogenate with cesium internal solution resulted in a large depolarization of the membrane potential (median 13.76 mV) which was larger than that caused by 11.4 mM K+.
source: Despite the addition of cesium the T. crassiceps homogenate still resulted in a large depolarization of the membrane potential (median 13.76, IQR 10.86–17.24 mV, N = 49 from 48 slices) which was larger than that caused by 11.4 mM K+ (p < 0.0001, Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunns' multiple comparison test, Figure 2B, C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Although K+ in the T. crassiceps homogenate may contribute to membrane depolarization, much of the effect is mediated by a different component.
source: Together, this indicates that although K+ in the T. crassiceps homogenate may contribute to membrane depolarization, much of the effect is mediated by a different component.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data comparing K+ and homogenate effects.

claim: The excitatory component of the T. crassiceps homogenate is a molecule smaller than 3 kDa.
source: This suggests that the excitatory component of the T. crassiceps homogenate is a molecule smaller than 3 kDa.
evidence: This is inferred from dialysis experiments shown in Figure 2D-E where dialysed homogenate (>3 kDa) had greatly reduced depolarizing effects.

claim: Brief application of total T. crassiceps E/S products was sufficient to cause neuronal depolarization (median 12.40 mV) significantly larger than that of the media control.
source: Brief application of total T. crassiceps E/S products using a soma directed puff was sufficient to cause neuronal depolarization (median 12.40 mV, IQR 9.94–14.07 mV, N = 7 from 3 slices) significantly larger than that of the media control (median –0.61 mV, IQR –0.80–0.35 mV, N = 7 from 2 slices, p ≤ 0.0001, Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparison test, Figure 2F, G, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: The T. crassiceps E/S product fraction larger than 3 kDa did not generate significant neuronal depolarization as compared to media control.
source: However, the T. crassiceps E/S product fraction larger than 3 kDa (median 1.25 mV, IQR 1.02–2.21 mV, N = 8 from 1 slice) did not generate significant neuronal depolarization as compared to media control (p = 0.17, Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparison test, Figure 2F, G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: Both T. crassiceps homogenate and T. crassiceps E/S products contain an excitatory component, which is a small molecule.
source: Together this set of experiments demonstrated that both T. crassiceps homogenate and T. crassiceps E/S products contain an excitatory component, which is a small molecule.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dialysis experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: 100 µM Substance P had no acute effect on the membrane potential of CA3 hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
source: We found, however, that 100 µM Substance P had no acute effect on the membrane potential of CA3 hippocampal pyramidal neurons (median 0.08 mV, IQR 0.01–0.12 mV, N = 5 from 1 slice, p = 0.0625, Wilcoxon signed rank test with theoretical median, Figure 3A, B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Blockade of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors with mecamylamine hydrochloride did not significantly alter the T. crassiceps homogenate induced depolarization.
source: Blockade of nAchRs with mecamylamine hydrochloride (10 µM) did not, however, significantly alter the T. crassiceps homogenate induced depolarization. The median T. crassiceps homogenate induced depolarization was 16.28 mV (IQR 13.54–23.63 mV) during baseline, 16.58 mV (IQR 11.21–24.50 mV) in the presence of mecamylamine hydrochloride, and 13.20 mV (IQR = 10.37–23.48 mV) following washout (N = 5 from 5 slices, p = 0.6914, Friedman test, Figure 3C, D, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Blockade of acid-sensing ion channels with amiloride did not significantly attenuate the effect of T. crassiceps homogenate.
source: Blockade of ASICs with the non-specific ASIC blocker amiloride (2 mM) did not, however, significantly attenuate the effect of the homogenate (Figure 3E), with the median T. crassiceps homogenate induced depolarization being 13.86 mV (IQR 11.00–16.48 mV) during baseline, 11.99 mV (IQR 4.97–19.03 mV) in the presence of amiloride, and 15.79 mV (IQR 13.25–24.67 mV) following washout (N = 10 from 10 slices, p = 0.1873, Friedman test, Figure 3E, F, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Glutamate receptor blockade significantly reduced the median T. crassiceps homogenate induced neuronal depolarization from 14.72 mV to 1.90 mV, which recovered to 14.37 mV following washout.
source: We found that GluR blockade significantly reduced the median T. crassiceps homogenate induced neuronal depolarization from 14.72 mV (IQR 13.39–15.68 mV) to 1.90 mV (IQR 1.09–2.21 mV), which recovered to a median value of 14.37 mV (IQR 7.32–16.38 mV) following washout (N = 9 from 9 slices, p ≤ 0.01, Friedman test with Dunn's multiple comparison test, Figure 3G, H, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: Application of glutamate receptor antagonists reduced the median total T. crassiceps E/S products-induced depolarization from 16.35 mV to 2.19 mV, which recovered to 16.43 mV following washout.
source: Similarly, for T. crassiceps E/S products we found that application of GluR antagonists reduced the median total T. crassiceps E/S products-induced depolarization from 16.35 mV (IQR 15.17–19.03 mV) to 2.19 mV (IQR 1.67–4.16 mV), which recovered to a median value of 16.43 mV (IQR 14.41–23.14 mV) following washout (N = 10 from 10 slices, p ≤ 0.01, Friedman test with Dunn's multiple comparison test, Figure 3I, J, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3I-J.

claim: The acute excitatory effects of both T. crassiceps homogenate and T. crassiceps E/S products are mediated through glutamate receptors.
source: These results indicate that the acute excitatory effects of both T. crassiceps homogenate and T. crassiceps E/S products are mediated through GluRs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the glutamate receptor blockade experiments shown in Figure 3G-J.

claim: Brief puffs of T. crassiceps homogenate delivered over the soma of iGluSnFR-expressing pyramidal neurons caused a robust increase in fluorescence (median 23.32%).
source: Brief puffs of T. crassiceps homogenate delivered over the soma of iGluSnFR-expressing pyramidal neurons caused a robust increase in fluorescence (median 23.32%, IQR 5.79% to 37.66%, N = 35 from 6 slices, Figure 4B, G, Figure 4—source data 1) when compared to puffs of aCSF (median 0.0012%, IQR –0.42% to 1.02%, N = 12 from 1 slice, p < 0.0001, Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparison test, Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B and 4G.

claim: Fluorescence increases were observed with puffs of T. crassiceps E/S products (median 11.69%).
source: Fluorescence increases were also observed with puffs of T. crassiceps E/S products (median 11.69%, IQR 2.94% to 15.85%, N = 10 from 2 slices, Figure 4C, G) although this did not reach statistical significance when compared to puffs of aCSF (median 0.0012%, IQR –0.42% to 1.02%, N = 12 from 1 slice, p = 0.16, Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparison test, Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C and 4G.

claim: iGluSnFR is sensitive to aspartate as well as glutamate.
source: iGluSnFR is also known to be sensitive to aspartate as well as glutamate (Marvin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marvin et al., 2013.

claim: Puffing aCSF containing 100 μM glutamate onto hippocampal pyramidal neurons expressing iGluSnFR resulted in significantly higher fluorescence (median 31.35%) compared to aCSF.
source: We found that puffing aCSF containing 100 μM glutamate (median 31.35%, IQR 15.35% to 54.92%, N = 14 from 2 slices, Figure 4E, G) or 100 μM aspartate (median 15.09%, IQR 11.12% to 33.12%, N = 5 from 1 slice, Figure 4F, G) onto hippocampal pyramidal neurons expressing iGluSnFR resulted in a significantly higher fluorescence as compared to aCSF (median 0.0012%, IQR –0.42% to 1.02%, N = 12 from 1 slice, Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparison test, p ≤ 0.05, Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4E and 4G.

claim: Puffing aCSF containing 100 μM aspartate onto hippocampal pyramidal neurons expressing iGluSnFR resulted in significantly higher fluorescence (median 15.09%) compared to aCSF.
source: We found that puffing aCSF containing 100 μM glutamate (median 31.35%, IQR 15.35% to 54.92%, N = 14 from 2 slices, Figure 4E, G) or 100 μM aspartate (median 15.09%, IQR 11.12% to 33.12%, N = 5 from 1 slice, Figure 4F, G) onto hippocampal pyramidal neurons expressing iGluSnFR resulted in a significantly higher fluorescence as compared to aCSF (median 0.0012%, IQR –0.42% to 1.02%, N = 12 from 1 slice, Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparison test, p ≤ 0.05, Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F and 4G.

claim: Puffing aCSF containing 100 μM glutamate during whole-cell current-clamp recordings elicited membrane depolarizations (median 15.05 mV) similar to those observed with T. crassiceps homogenate.
source: Similarly, puffing aCSF containing 100 μM glutamate (median 15.05 mV, IQR 11.12–18.71 mV, N = 6 from 1 slice, Figure 4H, I, Figure 4—source data 2) or 80 μM aspartate (median 7.75 mV, IQR 3.74–15.99 mV, N = 5 from 1 slice, Figure 4H, I) during whole-cell current-clamp recordings elicited membrane depolarizations which were similar those observed with T. crassiceps homogenate (median 13.76 mV, IQR 10.87–17.24 mV, N = 49 from 48 slices, Figure 4I) and E/S products (median 12.40 mV, IQR 9.94–14.07 mV, N = 7 from 3 slices, Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparison test, p > 0.05, Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4H-I.

claim: Puffing aCSF containing 80 μM aspartate during whole-cell current-clamp recordings elicited membrane depolarizations (median 7.75 mV) similar to those observed with T. crassiceps E/S products.
source: Similarly, puffing aCSF containing 100 μM glutamate (median 15.05 mV, IQR 11.12–18.71 mV, N = 6 from 1 slice, Figure 4H, I, Figure 4—source data 2) or 80 μM aspartate (median 7.75 mV, IQR 3.74–15.99 mV, N = 5 from 1 slice, Figure 4H, I) during whole-cell current-clamp recordings elicited membrane depolarizations which were similar those observed with T. crassiceps homogenate (median 13.76 mV, IQR 10.87–17.24 mV, N = 49 from 48 slices, Figure 4I) and E/S products (median 12.40 mV, IQR 9.94–14.07 mV, N = 7 from 3 slices, Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparison test, p > 0.05, Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4H-I.

claim: During imaging periods lasting up to 15 min with iGluSnFR-expressing neurons adjacent to a live T. crassiceps larva, fluorescence was stable, indicating no detectable oscillatory changes in ambient glutamate/aspartate.
source: During imaging periods lasting up to 15 min, fluorescence was stable, indicating no detectable oscillatory changes in ambient glutamate/aspartate on the timescales recorded (N = 2 slices, Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The median concentration of glutamate in the T. crassiceps homogenate was 119.9 μM.
source: We found that the median concentration of glutamate in the T. crassiceps homogenate and E/S products were 119.9 μM (IQR 73.41–153.2 μM, N = 5, Figure 5D, Figure 5—source data 1) and 72.32 μM (IQR 32.95–116.0 μM, N = 6, p = 0.1061, Mann–Whitney test, Figure 5D), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by glutamate assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The median concentration of glutamate in T. crassiceps E/S products was 72.32 μM.
source: We found that the median concentration of glutamate in the T. crassiceps homogenate and E/S products were 119.9 μM (IQR 73.41–153.2 μM, N = 5, Figure 5D, Figure 5—source data 1) and 72.32 μM (IQR 32.95–116.0 μM, N = 6, p = 0.1061, Mann–Whitney test, Figure 5D), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by glutamate assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The median concentration of aspartate in T. crassiceps homogenate was 25.8 μM.
source: The median concentration of aspartate in T. crassiceps homogenate and E/S products were 25.8 μM (IQR 16.5–35.1 μM, N = 3, Figure 5E) and 44.03 μM (IQR 17.56–84.74 μM, N = 3, p = 0.4000, Mann–Whitney test, Figure 5E), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by aspartate assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The median concentration of aspartate in T. crassiceps E/S products was 44.03 μM.
source: The median concentration of aspartate in T. crassiceps homogenate and E/S products were 25.8 μM (IQR 16.5–35.1 μM, N = 3, Figure 5E) and 44.03 μM (IQR 17.56–84.74 μM, N = 3, p = 0.4000, Mann–Whitney test, Figure 5E), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by aspartate assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: T. crassiceps larval homogenate and E/S products contain the excitatory amino acids glutamate and aspartate at concentrations that are sufficient to elicit neuronal depolarization.
source: Together, these findings suggest that T. crassiceps larval homogenate and E/S products contain the excitatory amino acids glutamate and aspartate at concentrations that are sufficient to elicit neuronal depolarization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the amino acid assay data in Figure 5D-E and the electrophysiology data.

claim: T. crassiceps larvae released a relatively constant median daily amount of glutamate, ranging from 41.59 to 60.15 µg/20 larvae, which showed no statistically significant difference across days 1–6.
source: T. crassiceps larvae released a relatively constant median daily amount of glutamate, ranging from 41.59 to 60.15 µg/20 larvae, which showed no statistically significant difference across days 1–6 (N = 3 per day, p = 0.18, Kruskal–Wallis test, Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by de novo production data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: T. crassiceps larvae released a relatively constant median daily amount of aspartate, ranging from 9.43 to 14.18 µg/20 larvae, which showed no statistically significant difference across days 1–6.
source: Similarly, T. crassiceps larvae released a relatively constant median daily amount of aspartate, ranging from 9.43 to 14.18 µg/20 larvae, which showed no statistically significant difference across days 1–6 (N = 3 per day, p = 0.28, Kruskal–Wallis test, Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by de novo production data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Both T. solium homogenate and T. solium E/S products caused membrane depolarization in human layer 2/3 pyramidal cells, which was sufficient to result in action potential firing.
source: Similarly to T. crassiceps, both T. solium homogenate (Figure 6A) and T. solium E/S products (Figure 6A) caused membrane depolarization, which was sufficient to result in action potential firing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Significant levels of glutamate were detected in both T. solium homogenate (46.4 μM) and the T. solium E/S products (722 μM).
source: Significant levels of glutamate were detected in both T. solium homogenate (46.4 μM, N = 1, Figure 6C, Figure 6—source data 1) and the T. solium E/S products (722 μM, N = 1, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by amino acid assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Aspartate levels were undetectable in the T. solium homogenate and low in the E/S products (15.3 μM).
source: Aspartate levels were, however, undetectable in the T. solium homogenate (N = 1, Figure 6C), and low in the E/S products (15.3 μM, N = 1, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by amino acid assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: T. solium larvae released a large amount of glutamate on the first day post-harvest (391.1 μM/20 larvae).
source: We found that, following harvest of live larvae, T. solium larvae released a large amount of glutamate on the first day post-harvest (391.1 μM/20 larvae, N = 1, Figure 6D), none on the second and third day in vitro (N = 1 each, Figure 6D), but produced significant amounts of glutamate de novo on days 4–6 (day 4: 131.9 μM/20 larvae, N = 1; day 5: 140.6 μM/20 larvae, N = 1; day 6: 158.8 μM/20 larvae, N = 1, Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by de novo production data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: T. solium larvae produced significant amounts of glutamate de novo on days 4–6 (day 4: 131.9 μM/20 larvae; day 5: 140.6 μM/20 larvae; day 6: 158.8 μM/20 larvae).
source: We found that, following harvest of live larvae, T. solium larvae released a large amount of glutamate on the first day post-harvest (391.1 μM/20 larvae, N = 1, Figure 6D), none on the second and third day in vitro (N = 1 each, Figure 6D), but produced significant amounts of glutamate de novo on days 4–6 (day 4: 131.9 μM/20 larvae, N = 1; day 5: 140.6 μM/20 larvae, N = 1; day 6: 158.8 μM/20 larvae, N = 1, Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by de novo production data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: T. solium larvae released aspartate in smaller amounts than glutamate on days 2 and 4–6 (day 2: 8.4 μM/20 larvae; day 4: 16.8 μM/20 larvae; day 5: 28.1 μM/20 larvae; day 6: 31.9 μM/20 larvae).
source: Aspartate was not detected on days 1 and 3 (N = 1 each, Figure 6D), but was observed to be released in smaller amounts than glutamate on days 2 and 4–6 (day 2: 8.4 μM/20 larvae, N = 1; day 4: 16.8 μM/20 larvae, N = 1; day 5: 28.1 μM/20 larvae, N = 1; day 6: 31.9 μM/20 larvae, N = 1, Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by de novo production data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: T. solium larvae continually release glutamate and aspartate into their immediate surroundings.
source: These results demonstrate that T. solium larvae continually release glutamate and aspartate into their immediate surroundings.
evidence: This is an inference based on the de novo production data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Cestode larval products cause neuronal depolarization and can initiate seizure-like events via glutamate receptor activation.
source: Here, we used patch-clamp electrophysiology, and calcium imaging in rodent hippocampal organotypic slice cultures and human acute cortical slices to demonstrate that cestode larval products cause neuronal depolarization and can initiate SLEs via glutamate receptor activation.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: T. crassiceps and T. solium larvae contain and release the excitatory amino acid glutamate and, to a lesser extent, aspartate.
source: Glutamate-sensing fluorescent reporters and amino acid assays revealed that T. crassiceps and T. solium larvae contain and release the excitatory amino acid glutamate and, to a lesser extent, aspartate.
evidence: This is supported by iGluSnFR imaging data in Figure 4 and amino acid assay data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The presence of cestode larvae in the brain can result in the generation of seizures.
source: Clinical evidence and animal models conclusively demonstrate that the presence of cestode larvae in the brain can result in the generation of seizures (Nash et al., 2015; Verastegui et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nash et al., 2015 and Verastegui et al., 2015.

claim: Taenia larvae have a direct excitatory effect on neurons via glutamatergic signalling.
source: In this study we have identified that Taenia larvae have a direct excitatory effect on neurons via glutamatergic signalling.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The central role of glutamatergic signalling in epileptogenesis has been conclusively shown using multiple cell culture, slice, and in vivo models of epilepsy.
source: This is important, as the central role of glutamatergic signalling in epileptogenesis has conclusively been shown using multiple cell culture (Sun et al., 2001; Sombati and Delorenzo, 1995; DeLorenzo, 1998), slice (Anderson et al., 1986; Stasheff et al., 1989; Ziobro et al., 2011), and in vivo models of epilepsy (Croucher and Bradford, 1990; Croucher et al., 1988; Rice and DeLorenzo, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on epilepsy models.

claim: Major causes of adult-acquired epilepsy beyond NCC are stroke, traumatic brain injury and CNS tumours.
source: Clinically, beyond NCC, other major causes of adult-acquired epilepsy are stroke, traumatic brain injury and CNS tumours (Hauser et al., 1940; Forsgren et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hauser et al., 1940 and Forsgren et al., 2005.

claim: In stroke, traumatic brain injury and CNS tumours, glutamatergic signalling and glutamate excitotoxicity are thought to be central to the pathogenic process.
source: In these other causes of acquired epilepsy, glutamatergic signalling, and glutamate excitotoxicity, are thought to be central to the pathogenic process.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about these conditions.

claim: Glutamate excitotoxicity occurs when depolarized, damaged, or dying neurons release glutamate, which activate surrounding neurons via NMDA and AMPA receptors, resulting in sustained neuronal depolarization, Ca2+ influx and the subsequent activation of signalling cascades and enzymes.
source: Glutamate excitotoxicity occurs when depolarized, damaged, or dying neurons release glutamate, which activate surrounding neurons via NMDA and AMPA receptors, resulting in sustained neuronal depolarization, Ca2+ influx and the subsequent activation of signalling cascades and enzymes.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about glutamate excitotoxicity, supported by citation to Ankarcrona et al., 1995.

claim: Glutamate excitotoxicity leads to cell death via necrosis and apoptosis, the further release of intracellular glutamate, and the propagation of the excitotoxic process to neighbouring cells.
source: These, in turn, lead to cell death via necrosis and apoptosis (Ankarcrona et al., 1995), the further release of intracellular glutamate, and the propagation of the excitotoxic process to neighbouring cells.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about glutamate excitotoxicity, supported by citation to Ankarcrona et al., 1995.

claim: Prolonged exposure to glutamate has been shown to cause hyperexcitability and seizures via multiple mechanisms, including enhanced intrinsic excitability and NMDA receptor-dependent disruption of GABAergic inhibition.
source: In the neurons that survive, the prolonged exposure to glutamate has been shown to cause hyperexcitability and seizures (Sun et al., 2001; DeLorenzo, 1998) via multiple mechanisms, including enhanced intrinsic excitability and NMDA receptor-dependent disruption of GABAergic inhibition (Lee et al., 2011; Terunuma et al., 2010; Buckingham et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on glutamate-induced hyperexcitability.

claim: It is possible that the brain's homeostatic mechanisms for taking up and metabolizing excess glutamate are overwhelmed by larval-derived glutamate released into the extracellular space.
source: Given our finding that cestode larvae contain and release significant quantities of glutamate, it is possible that the brain's homeostatic mechanisms for taking up and metabolizing excess glutamate are overwhelmed by larval-derived glutamate released into the extracellular space.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental findings.

claim: Similar glutamate-dependent excitotoxic and epileptogenic processes that occur in stroke, traumatic brain injury, and CNS tumours are likely to also occur in NCC.
source: Therefore, similar glutamate-dependent excitotoxic and epileptogenic processes that occur in stroke, traumatic brain injury, and CNS tumours are likely to also occur in NCC.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings and comparison to other conditions.

claim: Glioma typically presents with seizures in over 80% of patients.
source: Glioma, a common adult primary brain tumour, which typically presents with seizures in over 80% of patients (Santosh and Sravya, 2017), is an intriguing condition for comparison to NCC.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Santosh and Sravya, 2017.

claim: In glioma, tumour cells release glutamate into the extracellular space via the system xc−cystine–glutamate antiporter.
source: Here, the tumour cells themselves have been shown to release glutamate into the extracellular space via the system xc−cystine–glutamate antiporter (Buckingham et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Buckingham et al., 2011.

claim: There is compelling evidence that tumoural release of glutamate both causes seizures and favours glioma preservation, progression, and invasion in cases of malignant glioma.
source: Interestingly, there is compelling evidence that tumoural release of glutamate via this mechanism both causes seizures and favours glioma preservation, progression, and invasion in cases of malignant glioma (Sontheimer, 2008; Takano et al., 2001; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sontheimer, 2008; Takano et al., 2001; and Huang et al., 2013.

claim: It is possible that Taenia larvae in the brain utilize the release of glutamate and the induction of glutamate excitotoxicity to facilitate their growth and expansion, with the accompanying effect of seizure generation.
source: Analogously, it is possible that Taenia larvae in the brain utilize the release of glutamate and the induction of glutamate excitotoxicity to facilitate their growth and expansion, with the accompanying effect of seizure generation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on analogy to glioma.

claim: The death of Taenia larvae, or larval-derived cells, would result in the release of metabolic glutamate, further contributing to glutamate release and excitotoxicity.
source: In addition, the death of Taenia larvae, or larval-derived cells, would also result in the release of metabolic glutamate, further contributing to glutamate release and excitotoxicity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that larvae contain glutamate.

claim: In glioma, pharmacological agents (e.g. sulfasalazine), which block glutamate release have considerable potential as therapeutic agents for reducing seizure burden.
source: In the case of glioma, where the mechanism of glutamate release by tumour cells is known, pharmacological agents (e.g. sulfasalazine), which block glutamate release have considerable potential as therapeutic agents for reducing seizure burden in this condition.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about glioma treatment approaches.

claim: It is important that future work attempts to identify the molecular mechanisms underlying the Taenia-specific production of glutamate to inform the development of new therapeutic strategies.
source: Therefore, it is important that future work attempts to identify the molecular mechanisms underlying the Taenia-specific production of glutamate to inform the development of new therapeutic strategies to potentially reduce larval expansion and possibly treat seizures in NCC.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: In people with NCC, some experience acute seizures immediately following infection whilst others present with seizures months to years following initial infection.
source: In people with NCC, some experience acute seizures immediately following infection whilst others present with seizures months to years following initial infection (Adalid-Peralta et al., 2013; Verma et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Adalid-Peralta et al., 2013 and Verma et al., 2011.

claim: Multiple different, or possibly interacting, mechanisms might be involved in the epileptogenic process in NCC.
source: This suggests that multiple different, or possibly interacting, mechanisms might be involved in the epileptogenic process in NCC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clinical observation of variable seizure onset timing.

claim: Products from T. solium cysts mimicking viable cysts contain the enzyme glutamate dehydrogenase, which metabolizes glutamate, whilst products mimicking degenerating cysts do not.
source: A recent report has shown that products from T. solium cysts mimicking viable cysts contain the enzyme glutamate dehydrogenase, which metabolizes glutamate, whilst products mimicking degenerating cysts do not (Prodjinotho et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Prodjinotho et al., 2022.

claim: The glutamate levels the brain would be exposed to would be highest when a cyst dies and releases its contents into its immediate surroundings.
source: This predicts that the glutamate levels the brain would be exposed to would be highest when a cyst dies and releases its contents into its immediate surroundings.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding about glutamate dehydrogenase in viable vs degenerating cysts.

claim: Larval suppression of host inflammatory responses could help explain why many patients may remain asymptomatic for years following infection.
source: In support of this, larval suppression of host inflammatory responses could help explain why many patients may remain asymptomatic for years following infection.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the mechanism of delayed symptom onset.

claim: In the healthy brain parenchymal astrocytes are optimized to maintain extracellular glutamate at low concentrations.
source: In the healthy brain parenchymal astrocytes are optimized to maintain extracellular glutamate at low concentrations (Perea and Araque, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Perea and Araque, 2010.

claim: The inflammatory transition of astrocytes to a reactive phenotype is known to impede their ability to buffer uptake of extracellular glutamate.
source: However, the inflammatory transition of astrocytes to a reactive phenotype is known to impede their ability to buffer uptake of extracellular glutamate (Seifert et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seifert et al., 2010.

claim: It is conceivable that cyst-associated reactive astrocytosis may gradually erode the ability of homeostatic mechanisms to compensate for larvae derived extracellular glutamate resulting in delayed symptom onset in NCC.
source: It is therefore conceivable that cyst-associated reactive astrocytosis may gradually erode the ability of homeostatic mechanisms to compensate for larvae derived extracellular glutamate resulting in delayed symptom onset in NCC.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the mechanism of delayed symptom onset.

claim: Increased extracellular, parasite-derived excitatory amino acids such as glutamate, and perturbed glutamatergic signalling, possibly play a role in the development of seizures in NCC.
source: Nonetheless our findings provide the first evidence that, as is the case with the other common causes of adult-acquired epilepsy (i.e. stoke, traumatic brain injury, and glioma), increased extracellular, parasite-derived excitatory amino acids such as glutamate, and perturbed glutamatergic signalling, possibly play a role in the development of seizures in NCC.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings and comparison to other conditions.

claim: Rodent hippocampal organotypic brain slices were prepared using 6- to 8-day-old Wistar rats and C57BL/6 mice following the protocol originally described by Stoppini et al., 1991.
source: Rodent hippocampal organotypic brain slices were prepared using 6- to 8-day-old Wistar rats and C57BL/6 mice following the protocol originally described by Stoppini et al., 1991.
evidence: This describes the methodology used, supported by citation to Stoppini et al., 1991.

claim: Human cortical acute brain slices were obtained from patients undergoing elective neurosurgical procedures to treat refractory epilepsy.
source: For human cortical acute brain slices, brain tissue from temporal cortex was obtained from patients undergoing elective neurosurgical procedures at Mediclinic Constantiaberg Hospital to treat refractory epilepsy (two patients, details below).
evidence: This describes the source of human tissue used in the study.

claim: Larvae of T. crassiceps (ORF strain) were propagated in vivo by serial intraperitoneal infection of 5- to 8-week-old female C57BL/6 mice.
source: Larvae of T. crassiceps (ORF strain) were donated to us by Dr Siddhartha Mahanty (University of Melbourne, Melbourne, Australia) and propagated in vivo by serial intraperitoneal infection of 5- to 8-week-old female C57BL/6 mice.
evidence: This describes the methodology for maintaining T. crassiceps larvae.
